code.title: One find, three containers

followUps:
Half-open means the range includes the first position and excludes the last: [first, last). It is convenient because the size is just last - first, an empty range is first == last, and two ranges [a,b) and [b,c) join with no gap or overlap.

Example: a vector of 5 elements has begin() at index 0 and end() at index 5, one past the last. A loop for (it = first; it != last; ++it) needs no special case for empty input. end() also doubles as the natural "not found" result, but it must never be dereferenced.

C++20 ranges let you pass the whole container instead of a pair of iterators, for example std::ranges::sort(v), and add pipelines like v | views::filter(p) | views::transform(f). Iterators are still underneath, so the idea is unchanged, but calls are shorter and harder to get wrong.

Views are lazy: nothing is computed until you iterate, and no intermediate vector is built. Concepts also give clearer errors, since an algorithm states which iterator category it needs. Be careful that a view refers to the original data, so the data must outlive it.

code.title: Iterator category decides advance cost

followUps:
Because a set iterator is only bidirectional, so the library cannot jump to the middle. The generic std::lower_bound still does O(log N) comparisons but needs about N pointer steps to move around, so total time is O(N).

Example: in a set of 1,000,000 keys the algorithm would still perform roughly 20 comparisons, yet each advance walks node by node. Use the member s.lower_bound(x), which walks the tree and is truly O(log N). Free lower_bound is only fast on random access iterators like those of vector or deque.

Use std::iterator_traits<It>::iterator_category and compare it to the tag types, or in C++20 test concepts like std::random_access_iterator<It>. This is resolved at compile time, so there is no runtime cost.

if constexpr (std::random_access_iterator<It>)
    it += k;          // O(1)
else
    std::advance(it, k); // O(k)

Tags form an inheritance chain (random access derives from bidirectional, which derives from forward), so is_base_of_v also works to ask "at least this strong".

code.title: Checking strict weak ordering rules

followUps:
Yes. Comparing with a + b > b + a is a valid strict weak ordering on strings of digits, which is why it is the standard trick for "largest number from numbers". It is irreflexive because a+a > a+a is false, and it is asymmetric and transitive because it compares the numeric values of the two concatenations.

Example: for "9" and "34", "934" > "349", so 9 goes first. Two strings are equivalent only when both concatenations are equal, such as "3" and "3", and that relation is transitive.

Run the comparator on many small values and check the rules directly. For every pair and triple of sample values assert that comp(a,a) is false, that comp(a,b) and comp(b,a) are never both true, and that comp(a,b) && comp(b,c) implies comp(a,c).

That is O(N^3) for N samples, fine for N around 50. Add duplicates, negatives and extremes. Cheaper still: compile with -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG, which checks the ordering during sort and aborts when it finds comp(x,x) is true.

code.title: sort, stable_sort, partial_sort, nth_element

followUps:
The worst case is kept at O(N log N) by introsort: it starts as quicksort, counts the recursion depth, and when the depth passes about 2 log N it switches to heapsort, which is always O(N log N).

Small pieces (around 16 elements) are finished by insertion sort, which is fast on tiny ranges. Example: for N = 1,000,000 the depth limit is about 40, so a bad pivot sequence that would make quicksort O(N^2) is cut off and heapsort takes over. The cost is O(N log N) time and O(log N) stack space.

Add the original position to the sort key, so ties are broken by index. Then ordinary sort gives a stable result because no two elements compare equal.

vector<int> idx(n);
iota(idx.begin(), idx.end(), 0);
sort(idx.begin(), idx.end(), [&](int i, int j) {
    return a[i] != a[j] ? a[i] < a[j] : i < j;
});

Time O(N log N), extra space O(N) for the index array, the same as stable_sort's buffer.

code.title: lower_bound and upper_bound by hand

followUps:
Because lo + (hi - lo) / 2 never exceeds hi, while lo + hi can overflow a signed int when both are large. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C++ and gives a negative index in Java.

Example with 32-bit ints: lo = 1,500,000,000 and hi = 2,000,000,000 sum to 3.5 billion, above 2,147,483,647, so the midpoint turns negative. The safe form gives 1,750,000,000. Both forms are equal mathematically; only the safe one stays in range. In C++20 you can also use std::midpoint(lo, hi).

Binary search on the answer means searching over possible results instead of array positions, using a yes/no test that flips once from false to true. The loop is the same, with a[mid] < x replaced by !ok(mid).

long long lo = 0, hi = MAXV;      // answer in [lo, hi]
while (lo < hi) {
    long long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    if (ok(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1;
}

Example: smallest speed to finish N tasks in H hours; ok(speed) counts hours. Cost is O(log(range) x cost of ok).

code.title: remove does not shrink: erase-remove idiom

followUps:
Because unique only removes duplicates that sit next to each other, so equal values scattered through the range survive. Sorting puts all equal values together first.

Example: 3 1 3 with unique alone stays 3 1 3. After sorting it is 1 3 3 and unique gives 1 3. Remember to erase the tail afterwards. Sort plus unique costs O(N log N). If you must keep the first-seen order, use an unordered_set of seen values instead, at O(N) average time and O(N) space.

Erase-remove is O(N) in total; erasing one element at a time in a loop is O(N^2) for a vector, because each erase shifts all later elements left by one.

Example: removing 50,000 matching values from a vector of 100,000 can mean about 50,000 x 50,000 = 2.5 billion element moves in the loop, against about 100,000 moves with remove then one erase. Also, a loop that erases must use the iterator returned by erase, or it uses an invalid iterator. For list, erase in a loop is fine at O(1) each.

code.title: next_permutation step by step

followUps:
Use the factorial number system: each digit of k says which remaining element to take, which costs O(N^2) with a vector, instead of k calls at O(N) each.

k--; // zero-based
for (int i = n; i > 0; i--) {
    int f = fact[i - 1];
    out.push_back(pool[k / f]);
    pool.erase(pool.begin() + k / f);
    k %= f;
}

Example: the 3rd permutation of {1,2,3} has k = 2. 2 / 2! = 1 picks the element at index 1, which is 2. The remainder 0 then picks 1, and finally 3. Result: 2 1 3.

Run next_permutation on a 0/1 mask that has k ones, and take the positions of the ones as the chosen elements. Each distinct mask is exactly one combination.

vector<int> mask(n, 0);
fill(mask.begin(), mask.begin() + k, 1);
do { // pick i where mask[i] == 1
} while (prev_permutation(mask.begin(), mask.end()));

Start from the descending mask (ones first) and use prev_permutation, or start ascending (zeros first) with next_permutation. Example: n = 4, k = 2 gives C(4,2) = 6 masks. Cost is O(C(n,k) x n).

code.title: accumulate takes its type from init

followUps:
reduce is like accumulate but is allowed to add the elements in any order and in groups, so it can run in parallel with an execution policy. Because of that, the operation must be associative and commutative, and it uses the type of init the same way.

Example: std::reduce(std::execution::par, v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL) can split a million numbers across threads. For integer addition the result is identical. For doubles the order changes the rounding, so results can differ slightly between runs. Accumulate always goes strictly left to right, so it is the safe choice when order matters.

Use Kahan (compensated) summation, which carries a small correction for the bits lost in each addition, or sort by magnitude, or use long double. Plain summation can lose a lot when a big total meets small values.

double sum = 0, c = 0;
for (double x : v) {
    double y = x - c;
    double t = sum + y;
    c = (t - sum) - y;
    sum = t;
}

Example: adding 0.1 a million times with plain double drifts in the 6th decimal place; Kahan stays within a couple of ulps. Cost is still O(N) time and O(1) space. Do not compile with -ffast-math, which can remove the correction.

code.title: Lambda captures and common bugs

followUps:
A lambda is its own unique type, so the compiler knows exactly which code runs and can inline it. std::function erases the type behind a hidden pointer call, so every call is indirect and often allocates when the lambda is large.

Example: sorting 1,000,000 ints makes about 20 million comparisons. With a lambda each is a few inlined instructions, with std::function each is an indirect call that cannot be inlined, commonly 2 to 3 times slower overall. Use std::function only when you must store different callables in one variable.

Give the lambda an explicit self parameter, or store it in a std::function. The self-parameter form (C++14) avoids the std::function overhead, and C++23 adds this auto self.

auto fib = [](auto self, int n) -> int {
    return n < 2 ? n : self(self, n - 1) + self(self, n - 2);
};
cout << fib(fib, 10); // 55

The std::function<int(int)> f = [&](int n){ ... f(n-1) ... } version also works, but it is slower and the capture by reference must not outlive f. Note the trailing return type is required, since the compiler cannot deduce a recursive return type.

code.title: Inlined lambda vs function pointer in sort

followUps:
A function pointer comparator costs an indirect call per comparison, unless the compiler can see which function it is. A functor or lambda has a unique type, so its call is known at compile time and can be inlined.

Example: sorting 10 million ints with bool (*)(int,int) passed as the comparator is typically 10 to 30 percent slower than with less<int>, and qsort is slower still. The algorithm and its O(N log N) count of comparisons are identical; only the cost per comparison changes. Prefer a lambda or functor in hot paths.

Yes, with optimisation on, when the pointer is a compile-time constant at the call site. The compiler can then see through the pointer (constant propagation), and inline the target function.

Example: sort(v.begin(), v.end(), &cmp) where cmp is a plain function in the same file can be inlined at -O2, because after instantiation sort is called with a known pointer value. It usually fails when the pointer comes from a variable chosen at runtime, from a different translation unit without link-time optimisation, or when it is stored in a struct. Check with a benchmark instead of assuming.

code.title: Counting values <= x: sorted vector vs set

followUps:
Coordinate compression replaces large or sparse values by their rank among the sorted distinct values, so they fit in a small array index. Order is preserved, so comparisons still work.

vector<int> s = vals;
sort(s.begin(), s.end());
s.erase(unique(s.begin(), s.end()), s.end());
int id = lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x) - s.begin();

Example: values 1000, 5, 10^9, 5 become 1, 0, 2, 0 using sorted distinct list [5, 1000, 10^9]. A Fenwick tree then needs size 3, not 10^9. Cost is O(N log N) to build and O(log N) per lookup.

A Fenwick tree stores counts per compressed index, so a deletion is just an update with -1 at that value's index, the same O(log N) as an insert. The count of values at most x is the prefix sum.

void add(int i, int d) { for (i++; i <= n; i += i & -i) t[i] += d; }
int sum(int i) { int s = 0; for (i++; i > 0; i -= i & -i) s += t[i]; return s; }
add(id, +1);  // insert
add(id, -1);  // delete

Example: insert 5, 5, 9, delete one 5, then sum(rank of 5) = 1. All values must be known in advance for the compression.

code.title: A competitive programming template

followUps:
Use endl only when you really need the output flushed immediately. That is the case in interactive problems, where the judge waits for your line before replying, or when you print right before a possible crash.

Example: in an interactive problem, cout << 5 << endl; sends the query now. With '\n' the text may sit in the buffer and the judge times out. In normal problems, printing 200,000 lines with endl forces 200,000 flushes and can be several times slower than '\n'.

It replaces every int token with long long, so code that depends on the real int size breaks. It is quick to type, but it has costs.

Examples: int main() becomes long long main(), which some compilers reject. scanf("%d", &x) with a long long x reads only 4 of its 8 bytes, which is wrong. Every vector<int> uses double the memory (8 bytes instead of 4) and is slower to scan. Prefer using ll = long long; and use ll only where values can be large.

code.title: Stress test against a brute force

followUps:
Debug mode checks things that a release build skips for speed: indexing past the end with operator[], dereferencing end(), using an iterator after the container changed, and a bad comparator inside sort.

Example: v[5] on a vector of size 3 silently reads garbage in release, but aborts with a clear message under -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG. The cost is a big slowdown (often 5 to 10 times) and a different container layout, so use it for testing only, never for timing.

Shrink by removing parts of the failing input and keeping the removal only if the bug still shows. This is called delta debugging, and it is easy to do automatically.

Steps: try deleting half the elements, then a quarter, then single elements, and lower the values toward 0 or 1. Keep each change only when the two programs still disagree. Example: a failing array of 8 numbers often shrinks to 2 or 3 numbers. Also generate small inputs first (N up to 5 and values in a tiny range), so the first failure found is already close to minimal.
